planting.note: Divide rhizome offsets with independent roots in spring; this is the wild Bornean species behind the already-grown 'Purple Cloak' and 'Candy Sticks' selections, so unselected divisions can vary in petiole and leaf-back color.

directions: A Bornean rainforest-slope species grown for its sharply triangular, almost V-folded leaves held upright on tall, slender petioles rather than the broad arrow shape typical of most elephant ears. In habitat it roots over well-drained slopes and ridges, including basalt and limestone outcrops, and several stems can rise from a single spreading rhizome to form an architectural, open clump rather than a dense mound. This straight species is the source of two named selections already grown in the trade, 'Purple Cloak' and 'Candy Sticks,' both prized for petiole and leaf-underside color that the plain wild-type lacks. Grow in bright, filtered light with high humidity and a coarse, fast-draining aroid mix, since the upright growth habit shows stress quickly if the roots sit wet.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens Kew — Plants of the World Online

common_name: Candy Sticks Alocasia (Pink-Petioled Princeps Elephant Ear)

planting.note: Divide rooted basal offsets in spring; this sister selection to the already-grown 'Purple Cloak' is identified by its bright pink petioles rather than a purple leaf underside.

directions: A selection of the Bornean species Alocasia princeps named for its vivid bubblegum-pink petioles, which hold up triangular, mottled green-and-white leaves in a striking color pairing distinct from the plain green petioles of the wild type. Where the already-grown 'Purple Cloak' selection of this same species shows its color on the leaf underside, 'Candy Sticks' carries its contrast on the stem instead, making the two cultivars easy to tell apart even before the leaves fully unfurl. Growth is upright and clumping from a short rhizome, staying more compact than the straight species, and new leaves often emerge with heavier pink petiole color that moderates slightly as they mature. Provide bright, indirect light and steady humidity in a chunky, fast-draining aroid mix, and avoid low light, which dulls both the leaf mottling and the petiole color.
sources: Foliage Factory specialty aroid nursery reference

common_name: Borneo King Alocasia (Giant Rippled Odora-Borneo Giant Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown stock after frost danger passes in rich, moisture-retentive, well-drained soil; the rhizome is hardier than the top growth and can survive a cool winter where mulched heavily.

directions: A large-growing hybrid bred by crossing Alocasia odora with the massive 'Borneo Giant' selection of Alocasia macrorrhizos, combining the vigor and comparatively greater cold tolerance of odora with the huge, heavily rippled leaf size associated with Borneo Giant. Bright green, upright leaves can reach several feet long on a plant that grows quickly from a small division to a towering specimen in a single warm season, giving it outsized presence in a shaded tropical border or large container. Its rhizome is reported to survive outdoors at the cooler edge of Alocasia range when well mulched, even though the foliage itself is killed by frost and regrows from the root the following season. Give it rich, evenly moist soil, high humidity, and generous feeding during the growing season to support its rapid, large-scale growth.
sources: Gabriella Plants specialty aroid nursery reference

planting.note: Divide rhizome offsets once they carry independent roots; this Philippine endemic is still relatively uncommon in cultivation and is usually propagated from division rather than seed.

directions: A Philippine species endemic to Panay Island, named for its deeply undulated, almost subpinnatifid leaf margins that spread outward into pointed lobes resembling a bat's wings in flight. Dark green leaves are held in a wide, horizontal fan rather than the upright sagittate form typical of most Alocasia, giving the plant a distinctly different silhouette from jewel Alocasia grown for leaf color. It was first brought to wider hobbyist attention through Philippine aroid collectors and horticultural society plant shows before spreading into the broader specialty trade. Grow in bright, filtered light with high humidity and a chunky, fast-draining aroid mix, and avoid letting the rhizome sit wet, since root rot is the most common cause of loss in cultivation.
sources: Foliage Factory specialty aroid nursery reference
